overview: CGI Inc. is a Montreal-headquartered global IT and business consulting services firm founded in 1976, with approximately 94,000 consultants and professionals operating in a proximity-based delivery model across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. The company provides end-to-end digital services spanning strategic IT consulting and systems integration, managed IT and business process outsourcing, and proprietary intellectual-property (IP) software solutions, serving government, financial services, manufacturing/retail/distribution, communications/utilities, and health clients. CGI trades on both the TSX (GIB.A) and NYSE (GIB) and has grown historically through a disciplined 'Build and Buy' strategy combining organic contract wins with a long history of acquisitions.

business_model.summary: CGI earns revenue from three interlocking lines: (1) Business and strategic IT consulting & systems integration (~45% of FY2025 revenue) — project-based, higher variability; (2) Managed IT and business process services (~55% of FY2025 revenue) — long-term outsourcing contracts (often 5-10+ years) that are recurring/contractual and underpin backlog visibility; and (3) a smaller but growing layer of proprietary IP-based software solutions embedded within service engagements, which carries higher margins. Growth is driven by a 'Build and Buy' strategy: Pillar 1 (win/renew/extend contracts) and Pillar 2 (new large managed-services deals) represent organic 'Build'; Pillars 3 and 4 (metro-market and large transformational acquisitions) represent 'Buy' — CGI has been one of the most acquisitive consolidators in IT services, closing roughly 5-6 acquisitions in FY2025 alone (Daugherty, BJSS, Novatec, Momentum, Apside) plus further deals in FY2026 (OBS, Comarch Polska, Stratfield).

revenue_streams.name: Managed IT and business process services
Business & strategic IT consulting and systems integration

business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2B/B2G — large enterprises and government agencies; U.S. federal government alone is ~14% of revenue (a single IFRS-defined customer); government overall is the largest vertical at ~38% of revenue
business_model.geographic_mix: U.S. 32%, Canada 14%, France 14%, U.K. 14%, Germany 6%, Finland 6%, Sweden 4%, Rest of world 10% (FY2025 revenue distribution); nine operating/delivery segments: U.S. Commercial & State Government, U.S. Federal, Canada, Western & Southern Europe, U.K. & Australia, Scandinavia/Northwest/Central-East Europe, Germany, Finland/Poland/Baltics, and Asia Pacific delivery centers (India/Philippines)

competitive_position.market_position: CGI is a mid-sized global player relative to the largest IT services firms — FY2025 revenue of ~CAD$15.9B compares to Accenture (~$77B+), Capgemini (~$24B), TCS (~$30B), and Infosys (~$20B); it is nonetheless 'one of few firms with the scale, reach, and capabilities to meet clients' enterprise business and technology needs' per its own disclosure, and it has carved out a durable niche in North American and European public-sector/government outsourcing plus metro-market commercial consulting.

moat_factors.description: Managed IT and business process services contracts are typically long-dated (5-10+ years) and deeply embedded in client operations (especially government systems), creating high switching costs and a large (~$31.5B, ~2x revenue) backlog with multi-year visibility.

moat_factors.factor: Local/proximity delivery model combined with global delivery network
moat_factors.description: CGI differentiates via local relationships/accountability (consultants embedded near clients) blended with offshore/nearshore delivery centers (India, Philippines) for cost efficiency — a hybrid model distinct from pure offshore players (TCS/Infosys) or pure onshore boutiques.
Decades of government relationships, security clearances, and compliance infrastructure (CGI Federal) create a regulatory/relationship barrier to new entrants in sensitive government IT contracts.

Majority of consultants are owners via the Share Purchase Plan and Profit Participation Plan, which management credits with retention, delivery consistency, and the 'Management Foundation' track record of on-time, within-budget delivery.
Decades of M&A experience (hundreds of acquisitions since founding) give CGI a repeatable integration process, though this is a learned capability rather than a hard-to-replicate structural moat.
Scale lags Accenture and the largest Indian IT majors, limiting leverage in the very largest global transformation deals, though CGI competes effectively in metro and national-scale engagements.

weaknesses: Sub-scale versus Accenture, Capgemini, TCS and Infosys in global brand and bidding leverage for mega-deals
Revenue mix still skews toward people-intensive, time-and-materials-like delivery, which is the business model most exposed to AI-driven productivity/pricing compression
Heavy reliance on competitive bidding processes limits pricing power and contract terms
Limited own-IP/software scale relative to hyperscalers and software-first competitors, despite IP solutions being a stated growth priority
Client concentration in U.S. federal government (14% of revenue, counted as a single IFRS customer) creates outsized exposure to U.S. budget and policy cycles

growth_drivers: Continued 'Build and Buy' M&A consolidation — five to six bolt-on/metro-market and transformational acquisitions in FY2025 (Daugherty, BJSS, Novatec, Momentum, Apside) plus further deals in FY2026 (Online Business Systems, Comarch Polska, Stratfield), expanding AI/data analytics, UK engineering, and European consulting capabilities

AI and agentic AI positioning — global go-to-market alliances with OpenAI (including expanded Codex access, announced January and April 2026) and Google Cloud/Gemini Enterprise (expanded January 2026) aimed at embedding AI into managed services and consulting delivery; ~40% of consultants reported to have AI expertise; CGI DigiOps AI-powered delivery model marketed to deliver 'double-digit efficiency improvements' for clients
Large managed IT and business process services contract wins — Pillar 2 of strategy; backlog of ~$31.8B (1.9x annual revenue) as of Q3 FY2026 provides multi-year revenue visibility
Government modernization demand globally (digital citizen services, legacy system modernization) despite near-term U.S. federal spending headwinds

Capital return program — active share buybacks (NCIB; ~$1.26B repurchased in FY2025, ~$1.37B through nine months of FY2026) plus a newly initiated and growing quarterly dividend ($0.15 to $0.17/share) providing additional per-share value support
Cross-sell of IP-based 'platform as a service' solutions into existing managed-services relationships to lift margins over time

business.risk: AI-driven disruption of the traditional time-and-materials/staff-augmentation IT services model
business.description: The dominant narrative pressuring the whole sector (and CGI specifically) in 2025-2026: if generative/agentic AI lets smaller teams deliver the same output, the historical link between headcount, billable hours, and revenue weakens, threatening both growth and pricing power industry-wide.

U.S. federal government and its agencies represented 14.1% of FY2025 revenue (treated as a single IFRS customer); federal efficiency/cost-cutting initiatives and the fall 2025 government shutdown drove a period of organic decline (as low as -12%) in the U.S. Federal segment before a slow recovery through FY2026.

Significant revenue is won through competitive bids that limit CGI's ability to negotiate favorable terms; larger competitors with greater financial/geographic scale and lower-cost offshore platforms exert pricing pressure.

A heavy and continuous acquisition cadence (6+ deals in FY2025-26) creates ongoing integration, cultural-alignment, and management-distraction risk; failure to realize synergies could impair growth and profitability targets.

Success depends on hiring/retaining qualified IT professionals (including those with government security clearances) and maintaining high utilization rates; labor market tightness or AI-driven headcount reductions across the industry could affect morale/retention even as it potentially lowers delivery costs.

business.risk: Revenue mix shift between shorter-term SI&C projects and long-term managed services
business.description: Increased reliance on systems integration & consulting (SI&C) projects (versus managed services) increases quarter-to-quarter revenue variability.

financial.risk: Rising net debt and leverage from acquisitions
financial.description: Net debt rose from ~$1.8B (FY2024) to ~$3.45B (FY2025) to ~$3.68B (Q3 FY2026), pushing the net debt-to-capitalization ratio from 16.2% to over 26%, driven by the Daugherty/BJSS/Novatec/Apside acquisitions and continued buybacks; ROIC has declined from 16.0% (FY2024) to 13.4% (Q3 FY2026).

financial.risk: Currency exposure (CAD functional/reporting currency vs. USD, EUR, GBP, SEK revenue)
financial.description: The majority of revenue and costs are denominated in non-CAD currencies; FX contributed 3.8 points of FY2025's 8.4% reported revenue growth (vs. 4.6% constant-currency growth), and a stronger CAD or currency volatility can materially swing reported results even when underlying demand is flat.

financial.risk: Interest rate sensitivity on variable-rate debt and refinancing costs
financial.description: While a large portion of debt is fixed-rate (including a 2025 US$650M 5-year note issuance), CGI retains exposure to its variable-rate credit facility and future refinancing costs in a higher-for-longer rate environment.

financial.risk: Tax policy risk (Pillar Two, France surcharge)
financial.description: Effective tax rate rose to 26.5% in part due to a new French corporate tax surcharge in FY2026; global minimum tax (Pillar Two) implementation adds further complexity and potential rate volatility across CGI's many tax jurisdictions.

regulatory.description: Government budget cuts, contract terminations/stop-work orders, shutdowns, or new legislation affecting government service providers could materially reduce revenue given government is CGI's largest vertical (~38% of revenue).

regulatory.risk: Data privacy and AI regulation (GDPR and emerging AI-specific laws)
regulatory.description: Increasingly complex and divergent global privacy and AI governance regimes raise compliance costs and liability risk, particularly given CGI's access to clients' sensitive data and growing AI-embedded service delivery.

regulatory.risk: U.S. federal contracting compliance (including DEI certification requirements)
regulatory.description: A January 2025 executive order requires U.S. federal contractors to certify non-operation of DEI programs violating anti-discrimination law; non-compliance risk includes contract termination, suspension/debarment, and fines.

Management flags tariffs/trade wars as a source of inflationary pressure, capital market volatility, and potential client budget disruption, though CGI's service-based model is less directly exposed than goods-based businesses.

macro.risk: Enterprise discretionary IT spending slowdown / recession sensitivity
macro.description: A portion of CGI's revenue (SI&C/consulting projects) is discretionary and can be deferred or cancelled in an economic downturn; European deal-making delays (notably in the Nordics) and financial services/manufacturing vertical softness were cited in FY2026 as evidence of this sensitivity.

High inflation raises compensation costs; CGI may not always be able to pass these through to clients, particularly under benchmarking clauses in managed-services contracts that tie pricing to peer comparisons.

macro.risk: Credit market conditions affecting M&A financing
macro.description: CGI's growth strategy depends on continued access to affordable debt/equity financing for acquisitions; tighter capital markets or a credit rating downgrade would raise the cost of executing the Build and Buy strategy.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The global IT services/consulting industry is in the midst of an AI-driven repricing of the traditional staff-augmentation model: large peers (Accenture, TCS, Infosys, Capgemini) are simultaneously investing heavily in AI capabilities while facing investor skepticism about whether AI will cannibalize billable-hours revenue faster than it creates new demand. Government IT modernization and AI adoption remain durable secular demand drivers, but discretionary enterprise consulting spend is more cyclical and currently soft in parts of Europe (Nordics) and in US federal (post-shutdown, efficiency-driven budget cuts).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — the large managed-services/outsourcing backlog (~$31.8B, ~1.9x revenue) provides significant revenue visibility and downside cushion, but the SI&C/consulting portion of the business is discretionary and cyclical, and bookings/book-to-bill have softened recently (100.1% in Q3 FY2026 vs. 119.2% a year-ago quarter high).
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — rising net debt (~$3.7B) and a capital-intensive acquisition strategy make CGI somewhat sensitive to the cost of debt financing, though most debt is currently fixed-rate.
key_input_costs: Third-party software licensing and AI model costs (OpenAI, Google Cloud)

recent_developments.event: Stock has fallen roughly 40-45% over the trailing 12 months on investor fears that generative/agentic AI will disrupt the legacy IT consulting/staff-augmentation model; FY2026 trading range on NYSE fell as low as the $59-65 area versus prior highs near $122.

Q3 FY2026 results: revenue of $4.19B (+2.5% YoY reported, +1.3% constant currency), adjusted diluted EPS of $2.29 (+9.0% YoY), book-to-bill of 100.1% in-quarter (108.1% trailing twelve months), backlog of $31.8B (1.9x revenue); growth deceleration versus the high-9%/11% YoY growth quarters of FY2025.

Leadership transition: President/CEO François Boulanger (30 years at CGI, including prior CFO/COO/CEO roles) retired; Tim Hurlebaus — previously President/COO overseeing the U.S., U.K. and Australia (nearly half of company revenue) — named President and CEO, explicitly amid the AI-fear-driven share price decline (per Bloomberg reporting).
Expanded global alliance with OpenAI, gaining early access to Codex agentic AI capabilities, joint go-to-market efforts, and training programs.
Acquired Stratfield, LLC (Atlanta-based management/technology consulting firm, ~200 consultants).
Announced new global go-to-market alliance with OpenAI and expanded alliance with Google Cloud (Gemini Enterprise/Gemini 3) to embed agentic AI into managed IT and business services.
Acquired Comarch Polska SA (Poland, ~460 professionals) and Online Business Systems (Canada/U.S., ~350 professionals).

Q2 FY2026 results missed consensus in USD terms (EPS $1.63 vs. $1.66 est.; revenue $2.99B vs. $3.11B est.), with stock dropping ~12-13% intraday; management attributed the miss to Nordic decision-making delays and slow U.S. Federal contract ramp-up following the fall 2025 government shutdown.

Completed five acquisitions during fiscal 2025 — Daugherty Systems ($343M, AI/data analytics), BJSS ($1,255.6M, UK engineering/tech consultancy — CGI's largest acquisition in the period), Novatec (Germany/Spain), Momentum Technologies (Quebec), and Apside-Advance (France, $229.9M) — alongside initiating a quarterly dividend ($0.15/share, raised to $0.17/share in Nov 2025) for the first time.

guidance.as_of: Q3 FY2026 earnings (July 29, 2026) and FY2025 annual results (November 5, 2025)

items.target: No explicit numeric full-year guidance disclosed; Q2 FY2026 call implied ~$3.09B USD for Q3 FY2026 (consensus-referenced, not formal company guidance)
items.vs_prior: not applicable - CGI does not publish formal quarterly/annual revenue or EPS guidance ranges
items.notes: CGI does not provide formal forward revenue/EPS guidance; management instead emphasizes bookings, book-to-bill (trailing-twelve-month target >100%), and backlog as leading indicators. Actual Q3 FY2026 revenue (CAD $4.19B / USD equivalent) came in with EPS exceeding the informally referenced analyst figure.

Stated long-standing management objective; actual trailing-twelve-month book-to-bill was 108.1% in Q3 FY2026, down from a 110.4% full-year FY2025 figure and well below the 119.2% single-quarter peak in Q4 FY2025, signaling some deceleration in new bookings momentum.

items.target: No explicit numeric target; historically managed in the mid-to-high teens
items.notes: Margin has been broadly stable in the 16-16.6% range across recent quarters despite revenue growth deceleration, reflecting cost discipline and the mix benefit of the Build and Buy strategy.

items.target: Continue NCIB share buybacks (up to 10% of public float annually) and grow the quarterly dividend
items.vs_prior: raised (dividend increased from $0.15 to $0.17/share in Nov 2025)
items.notes: Dividend initiated in FY2025 (first in company history) and raised in FY2026; buybacks continued at pace (~$1.37B repurchased through nine months of FY2026) even as net debt and leverage have risen from acquisitions.

items.target: Active acquisition pipeline described as including 'both large and niche targets'
items.notes: Management reiterated on the Q3 FY2026 call that the balance sheet remains positioned to support further Build and Buy acquisitions despite elevated net debt-to-capitalization (~26.6%).

guidance.management_commentary: New CEO Tim Hurlebaus has framed CGI's AI strategy around 'generative and agentic AI, which relies on industry-specific expertise,' arguing CGI's proximity model and deep industry knowledge differentiate it from commoditized AI tooling. Management acknowledged organic constant-currency growth remains modest (1.3% in Q3 FY2026) and attributed recent softness to temporary factors — European (especially Nordic) decision-making delays and slower-than-expected U.S. Federal contract ramp-up following the fall 2025 government shutdown — while expressing confidence in a 'gradual improvement' trajectory, a record trailing-twelve-month bookings level (~CAD $18B), and a reported pipeline up over 180%.

bull_case: Massive ~$31.8B backlog (1.9x annual revenue) from long-dated managed-services contracts provides multi-year revenue visibility and a cushion against short-term demand softness

Stock has fallen ~40-45% over the trailing year largely on sector-wide 'AI will destroy IT services' fears rather than company-specific fundamental deterioration — adjusted EPS actually grew double digits YoY in Q3 FY2026 even as reported revenue growth decelerated, creating a potential valuation disconnect for long-term investors

New alliances with OpenAI (Codex) and Google Cloud (Gemini Enterprise) position CGI to monetize AI as a service enabler for its large enterprise/government client base rather than being disintermediated by it; management claims ~40% of consultants already have AI expertise

Proven, decades-long 'Build and Buy' consolidation playbook continues to add capabilities and scale (6+ acquisitions across FY2025-26) while the company simultaneously initiated and is growing its first-ever dividend alongside continued meaningful buybacks

Diversified, sticky government and large-enterprise client base with high switching costs in outsourced/managed IT contracts, cushioning against the kind of rapid AI-driven commoditization that is more acute in pure staff-augmentation/offshore models
bear_case: The core bear thesis — that generative/agentic AI structurally erodes the people-hours-to-revenue link underlying traditional IT services and consulting pricing — is exactly the risk the market has been pricing in via the stock's sharp de-rating, and it is not yet clear CGI's AI alliances will offset pricing/volume pressure on legacy SI&C and managed-services work

Organic constant-currency growth has decelerated sharply (from ~8% in FY2025 to just 1.3% in Q3 FY2026) with book-to-bill trending down from FY2025 peaks, suggesting demand softness beyond temporary one-offs

U.S. federal government exposure (~14% of revenue, concentrated in a single IFRS-defined customer) remains vulnerable to further budget cuts, efficiency-driven contract reductions, and shutdown-related disruption

Rising leverage from an aggressive acquisition cadence has pushed net debt from ~$1.8B to ~$3.7B and net debt-to-capitalization from ~16% to ~27% in roughly 18 months, while ROIC has declined (16.0% to 13.4%), raising questions about capital discipline and returns on the 'Buy' half of the growth strategy
Fresh CEO transition (effective May 2026) introduces execution/strategy uncertainty at precisely the moment the company must prove its AI positioning thesis to a skeptical market
